metadata.title: An Ogilvy Lens on Threadline — Raksha
metadata.ogilvy_note: Food for thought — not a grade. Ogilvy is one lens among several, running alongside the course rubric. The maker decides.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN — ClaudeComposerAsk. Liam asks the Ogilvy question.
beats.narration_text: Raksha's Threadline pitch. An adaptive fashion market intelligence platform — consumer signals processed, ranked product opportunities ready before a brand spends a dollar on research. What would David Ogilvy ask about it?

props.command: I just watched Raksha's Threadline pitch — an adaptive fashion market intelligence platform built on 2,353 real consumer signals, with ranked product opportunities already live. What do David Ogilvy's principles say about how this pitch frames the work? Not a score, not a verdict. Just the questions a great ad man would ask.

beats.role_note: Show the actual Slide 1, then rebuild as Brutalist. Establish who Raksha is and what the pitch claims.
beats.narration_text: Let's start with what Raksha built. Slide 1 — Threadline, adaptive fashion market intelligence. The cover carries the origin story: an internship at a cancer detection startup, noticing people couldn't find clothing that worked for their bodies after treatment. That's the problem, and it's personal.

beats.role_note: Show the actual Slide 2, then rebuild as Brutalist. The market scale, the human voice in the data.
beats.narration_text: Slide 2 — The Problem. Fifteen to twenty billion dollar market. Thirty-five million consumers. One hundred sixty-eight thousand surgeries annually that fundamentally change what someone can wear. One brand focus group costs twenty thousand dollars and takes six weeks. And on this slide, a real quote from a verified Reddit post: 'Help me. I cannot make one more Amazon return. I'm weeks out from surgery and I'm looking for something that actually works.' That's the data. That's also the entire pitch in two sentences.

beats.act: LENS 1 — The Big Idea: Where Does It Live?
beats.role_note: Show Slide 7 (competition), rebuild, ask: the single differentiator is already written — does it lead?
beats.narration_text: Slide 7 — the competition slide. Here's the sentence that does the most work in this deck: 'Our competitors sell clothing. Threadline sells the intelligence that tells any brand — including them — what to build next.' Ogilvy wouldn't write a line until he could state the single differentiator in one plain sentence. Raksha already wrote it. The question worth sitting with: it lives six slides in. What if it led?

beats.act: LENS 2 — Story Appeal: The Reddit Quote
beats.role_note: The verified Reddit post is a Hathaway eyepatch moment — specific, dated, real. Does it get its own beat?
beats.narration_text: There's a real, verified Reddit post in this pitch: 'Help me. I cannot make one more Amazon return. I'm weeks out from surgery and I'm looking for something that actually works.' Ogilvy called moments like this story appeal — one concrete, specific detail that makes everything else credible. The Hathaway eyepatch was a man in a shirt ad with one eye covered. Nobody needed to explain why it was interesting. This quote has the same quality. What if it was the first thing in the pitch — before the market size, before the pipeline — just this?

beats.role_note: The market numbers are specific and strong. Ogilvy ran research first and showed it. Which study backs these?
beats.narration_text: The market numbers on Slide 2 are specific and strong — fifteen to twenty billion, thirty-five million consumers, one hundred sixty-eight thousand surgeries. Ogilvy ran research first and showed where it came from. Which report puts the adaptive clothing market at fifteen to twenty billion? Which dataset has the surgery count? A source line under each figure doesn't slow the pitch down — it gives the number somewhere to stand. The audience already wants to believe these numbers. A citation lets them.

beats.act: LENS 4 — The Close: One Ask or Three?
beats.role_note: Show Slide 10 (The Ask), rebuild, ask: which of the three asks does this audience walk away wanting to do?
beats.narration_text: Slide 10 — The Ask. 'Stop guessing what adaptive customers need. Start knowing.' Then three things: a pilot partner within sixty days, a developer to automate the manual pipeline, and an introduction to someone in the field. Ogilvy: the close should be specific enough to act on. The pilot partner ask has a timeline, a scope, and a deliverable — it's the clearest of the three. The question worth sitting with: do the other two asks sharpen it, or soften it?

beats.role_note: Not a verdict: the reusable lens set for Raksha's next draft.
beats.narration_text: Not a verdict — a lens set. Four questions to carry to the next draft. One: your big idea is on Slide 7 — what if it led? Two: the Reddit quote has the quality of a Hathaway eyepatch — does it have its own moment? Three: where did the market numbers come from? Four: three asks on Slide 10 — which one does your audience walk away wanting to do? These are Ogilvy's questions. The pitch decides which ones matter.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take your deck into Claude and try this: here are four Ogilvy questions about my pitch. For each one: which specific slide is most directly in play, and what's one alternative frame to consider — not a correction, just another angle. The goal is not to score the pitch. Ogilvy is one lens. The course rubric is another.
